corrections.source_says: The extraction omits relevant narrative-influence and local semantic-distance results. Transience asymmetry is HA mean 0.484, 95% CI [0.432, 0.537], n = 97 stories, versus HH mean 0.300, 95% CI [0.233, 0.370], n = 36 stories, with Cliff’s δ = 0.397 (Table 8). Table 3 also reports human-to-AI transience −1.02 and uptake 30.0%, versus human-to-human transience −0.83 and uptake 17.2%; its values are story-level clustered means. Novelty–resonance coupling slopes are HA 1.217, 95% CI [1.184, 1.250]; HH 1.066, 95% CI [1.003, 1.128]; and AA 0.956, 95% CI [0.913, 0.999] (§5.3). Adjacent semantic distance is HA 0.316, AA 0.296, and HH 0.287, with HA minus HH Δ = 0.0299, p < .0001 (§5.2). Record these as distinct output-scored measures, using other where appropriate for narrative-process constructs; adjacent-turn distance is local dissimilarity, not diversity across independent writers’ output sets. The within-HA resonance means (human −0.796 versus LLM −2.07) can be retained as author-role context with question none, not as an assistance-effect estimate. Form-spec.md Rule 7 requires coverage of relevant output outcomes rather than only the three currently listed.

confirmed: Read the entire local markdown (including Appendix A) and extracted text from all PDF pages. The document is arXiv:2609.07920v2, dated 9 Sep 2026, with 15 pages; the form’s title and author list match the title page (PDF p. 1).

Appendix A is included on PDF pp. 12–15: recruitment/preprocessing, generation and scoring, qualitative examples, diagnostics, valence descriptives in Table 7, and complete asymmetry estimates in Table 8. The form’s supplement description is supported.

The main comparison is a reused HA cohort, a separately recruited HH cohort, and AA simulations; HH recruitment excludes HA participants. No random assignment of people between partner types or LLM configurations is reported. quasi_people, observational context, core no, and null randomized-person counts are supported (PDF p. 3, §3.1; p. 12, Appendix A.1).

The paper reports 97 HA participants and 72 HH participants. Both reported human cohorts exceed 50 people; the HH count of 36 is stories, not people. AA comprises 80 model-generated stories and supplies no human participant count (PDF p. 3, §3.1 and Table 1).

Table 1 explicitly describes the final analytic corpus and distinguishes stories, exchanges, and turns; Table 7 counts scored turns, not people. Initial recruitment and exclusion counts are not supplied (PDF p. 3, §3.2 and Table 1 caption; p. 12, Appendix A.1; p. 14, Table 7).

Participants were mostly students at one university; HH participants were university or graduate students in English-taught Aarhus University programs, participating voluntarily without compensation (PDF p. 3, §3.1; p. 10, Limitations and Ethics Statement).
The storytelling instructions allow 10 exchanges; analyzed HA stories had 9 full exchanges. These are exchange counts, not elapsed task duration (PDF p. 3, §§3.1–3.2).

The listed generation models match the PDF: gpt-4.1-2025-04-14, claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct. Human turns were spell-corrected with gpt-4o-mini before scoring; that is preprocessing, not HH participants receiving assistance during writing (PDF p. 3, §3.1; p. 12, Appendix A.1–A.2).

Novelty is scored on produced turns using google/gemma-4-31B and contextual minus context-free mean token surprisal; less negative values indicate greater contextual novelty. Resonance is novelty minus transience. These are computational output measures, not self-reports or human creativity ratings (PDF p. 5, §4.4, Eqs. (4)–(6)).

S1-O1 reported numbers exactly match Table 8: HA novelty asymmetry 0.828, 95% CI [0.732, 0.926], n = 97 stories; HH 0.355, 95% CI [0.284, 0.428], n = 36 stories; Cliff’s δ = 0.591 (PDF p. 15, Novelty rows).

S1-O2 reported numbers exactly match the text: human mean Novelty −1.82 and 30.2% of turn-information explained by prior context; LLM −2.65 and 52.8%; p < .0001. These are within-HA author-role results (PDF p. 7, §5.3, Humans contribute higher novelty and resonance in HA stories).

S1-O3 reported numbers exactly match Table 8: HA resonance asymmetry 1.290, 95% CI [1.149, 1.432], n = 97 stories; HH 0.605, 95% CI [0.482, 0.733], n = 36 stories; Cliff’s δ = 0.572 (PDF p. 15, Resonance rows).

Table 8 defines asymmetry as the per-story absolute difference between writer-slot mean scores, and its caption explicitly says Cliff’s δ compares HA against each baseline. The form correctly distinguishes these gaps from overall story creativity (PDF p. 6, Eq. (7); p. 15, Table 8 caption).
The one_line_finding is supported: HA versus HH novelty asymmetry is 0.828 versus 0.355, and within HA human versus LLM novelty is −1.82 versus −2.65, p < .0001 (PDF p. 15, Table 8; p. 7, §5.3).

This is an empirical corpus comparison, not a review or meta-analysis; the empty synthesis estimates and null synthesis study/effect counts are appropriate (PDF pp. 3–8, Datasets, Methods, and Results).
summary: The paper supports observational context, with no reported randomized people study, and its quoted novelty/resonance statistics match the PDF. Corrections concern the derived total, outcome coding and completeness, exclusions, sample overlap, and missing metadata.
